description: I'm Divya Sri chartered accountant from India who has profound love for space
summary:
When we explore space, we cannot bring everything back. Abandoned but Not Forgotten tells the stories of the equipment NASA has left across the solar system, for school-age students. It has three parts: a 25-minute narrated animated documentary, a 30-second trailer, and an interactive web app where students click a world, zoom in, and explore what we left there.

The story is told in three chapters. “Still on Duty” covers what was left to keep working, like the laser mirrors on the Moon, the Voyagers and the Mars rovers. “Too Heavy to Carry Home” covers what had to stay, like the Moon buggies and retired Mars explorers. “We Were Here” covers what was left as a memory, like the Golden Record and a family photo on the Moon. For each object we show why it was sent, what it discovered, where it is now and why it still matters. Every fact was checked against NASA pages. We end by asking students what they would leave behind, and how they would make sure it does no harm.
details:
What it does
Abandoned but Not Forgotten helps school students discover the equipment NASA has left across the solar system, and why it still matters. It has three parts. A 25-minute narrated animated documentary tells the story in three chapters. A 30-second trailer invites students in. An interactive web app lets them explore on their own: they click a world, zoom in, turn the Moon or Mars globe, and open a pin to read what was left there, when, what it did and how it helped us.

How it works
The film mixes paper cut-out and pixel-art animation with real NASA photographs, so students see the actual spacecraft and astronauts. A documentary “camera” overlay shows the date, mission and location of each scene. Each object ends with a closing note and a “since” clock, such as “On the Moon since 1969 · 57 years”. The app is a single web page with real NASA maps of the Moon and Mars, NASA photographs, and three filters, one for each chapter.

Benefits and intended impact
Most students know about the Moon landings but not about what we left behind. The project shows that much of it is still working (the laser mirrors on the Moon), still teaching us (old moonquake recordings), or still carrying a message (the Golden Record). It also faces the cost: every machine we leave is also waste, on other worlds and around Earth. It ends by asking students what they would leave behind and how they would make sure it does no harm, to start a classroom conversation about exploring responsibly. Teachers can show the whole film, one chapter, or let students explore the app themselves.

Tools we used
Claude (Anthropic) generated the animation code, the app’s code and the drawn visuals. The animation was written in HTML and JavaScript and rendered to video with Playwright and FFmpeg. Earth’s coastlines come from Natural Earth map data, drawn with the d3-geo library. Canva was used for the voice-over, subtitles, music and final assembly. The app is hosted on GitHub Pages and the videos on YouTube.

How it is creative
Instead of listing hardware, we sorted it by why it was left: to keep working, because it was too heavy to bring home, or as a memory. That turns a list of objects into a story about people, choices and responsibility. The animation style is playful for young viewers, but every spacecraft is shown through real NASA images.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: every fact was checked against official NASA pages, and anything we could not confirm was removed.
  • Age: plain language, short scenes, English subtitles, and a question that invites discussion rather than a lecture.
  • Honesty about AI: a visible watermark on every frame and on the app, and no NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers were generated; those that appear are inside genuine NASA photographs.
  • Access: the app works on phones and computers, needs no sign-in, and its pins can also be chosen from a list below each world.

Youtube video link: https://youtu.be/al50pBo4rgI?si=YF6hm-RkCrMkxlJ0
